courses.courseDescription: The scientific content of this course includes: an introduction to numerical analysis, error estimation, solving non-linear equations, interpolation, theories for validating results, numerical integration and differentiation, solving systems of linear equations, matrix analysis methods, an introduction to solving ordinary differential equations, and Gaussian quadratures
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to: • Recognize the importance of using numerical methods to solve various scientific problems. • Explain interpolation methods, numerical integration and differentiation, and matrix analysis methods. • Identify the fundamental principles for solving systems of linear equations and ordinary differential equations. • Apply numerical methods to solve diverse scientific problems, finding approximate solutions to presented issues.
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Define fundamental concepts in numerical analysis, such as error estimation and solving non-linear equations. • Explain methods of interpolation, numerical integration and differentiation, and matrix analysis methods. • Identify the basic principles for solving systems of linear equations and ordinary differential equations. Intellectual Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Analyze the validity of numerical results to ensure their accuracy and reliability. • Interpret the differences between various numerical methods for solving the same problem and choose the most appropriate one. • Compare Gaussian quadratures with other numerical integration methods. Professional and Practical Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Apply numerical methods to solve non-linear equations and systems of linear equations. • Use interpolation techniques to approximate function values. • Calculate integrals and derivatives numerically using appropriate methods. Transferable Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Formulate real-world mathematical and engineering problems into numerically solvable problems. • Work efficiently within a team to discuss and apply numerical methods to complex problems. Communicate effectively about numerical methods and results with colleagues and specialists

courses.courseDescription: The course content includes: mechanical extensors and their types, Kayla's theory, extensor fields, stress analysis, fracture and strain, current flow, fundamental laws of continuum mechanics, and applications to viscosity and fluidity
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, the student will be able to: • Identify mechanical extensors. • Explain mechanical extensors and their types. • Recognize Kayla's theory.
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding Level • Defines mechanical extensors and their various types. • Explains the core principles of Kayla's theory. Cognitive Skills Level • Analyzes extensor fields and their effects. • Differentiates between fracture and strain in materials. Professional and Practical Skills Level • Applies fundamental laws of continuum mechanics to problem-solving. • Evaluates the applications of viscosity and fluidity in practical scenarios. General and Transferable Skills Level • Presents stress analysis results clearly. • Collaborates in discussing and interpreting current flow.

courses.courseDescription: The scientific content of this course includes: inverse functions, derivatives of inverse functions, derivatives of hyperbolic, inverse hyperbolic, and inverse trigonometric functions, and the relationship between inverse hyperbolic functions and the logarithmic function. It also covers various forms of L'Hôpital's Rule for limits. Integration methods include integration by substitution, by parts, and by partial fractions, along with applications of definite integrals. The course then moves to functions of several variables, partial derivatives, the chain rule, the equation of the tangent plane to a surface and its normal line, maxima and minima, and Taylor and Maclaurin expansions in two variables. Finally, it covers multiple integrals: double and triple integrals in Cartesian and polar coordinates, and triple integrals in Cartesian, cylindrical, and spherical coordinates
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to: • Identify different functions and their derivatives. • Grasp various integration methods and partial derivatives. • Analyze the relationships between these concepts within a unified framework of knowledge
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Identify inverse functions, hyperbolic functions and their derivatives, and the different forms of L'Hôpital's Rule. • Explain various integration methods (by substitution, by parts, by partial fractions) and their applications to definite integrals. • Determine the concepts of functions of several variables, partial derivatives, and the chain rule. Intellectual Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Analyze the relationships between inverse hyperbolic functions and the logarithmic function. • Interpret the concept of the tangent plane and normal line, and the maximum and minimum values for multivariable functions. • Distinguish between different types of multiple integrals in Cartesian, polar, cylindrical, and spherical coordinates. Professional and Practical Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Apply differentiation rules to inverse, hyperbolic, and inverse trigonometric functions. • Use multiple integration methods to calculate double and triple integrals in different coordinate systems. • Calculate Taylor and Maclaurin expansions for functions of two variables. Transferable Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Formulate clear and organized solutions for complex mathematical problems in calculus. • Work efficiently within a team to discuss and clarify mathematical concepts with each other. • Communicate effectively about mathematical methods and results with colleagues and specialists

courses.courseDescription: This course delves into fluid statics, beginning with the main equation of fluid statics and exploring static forces on submerged planar and curved surfaces. It then transitions to fluid dynamics, introducing Lagrangian and Eulerian systems and analyzing particle derivatives and acceleration in both Cartesian and cylindrical coordinate systems. Key concepts like streamlines, pathlines, and streaklines are covered, leading into fundamental principles such as Bernoulli's theorem and the calculation of dynamic fluid pressure. Practical applications, including the Pitot tube and Venturi meter, are discussed alongside the essential continuity and motion equations. Further topics include vorticity and circulation, Stokes' flow equation, and the use of the complex potential function to understand phenomena like sources, sinks, and their duality. The course concludes with advanced concepts such as the circle theorem and Blasius' theorem
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, the student will be able to: • Identify the properties of fluids (real and ideal fluids) and their potential energy. • Understand the fundamental forces resulting from fluid motion. • Classify flow in pipes and open channels and study energy loss during flow
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding Level • Identifies fundamental concepts of number theory. • Explains relationships between different mathematical systems. Cognitive Skills Level • Analyzes complex problems using mathematical logic. • Compares various mathematical theories and models. Professional and Practical Skills Level • Applies mathematical tools and software to solve problems. • Designs innovative solutions for technical challenges. General and Transferable Skills Level • Communicates effectively about complex scientific ideas. • Collaborates within a team to complete research projects

courses.courseTitle: Software for Mathematical and Statistical Applications
courses.courseDescription: The scientific content of this course includes: an introduction to symbolic computational software packages (e.g., Mathematica), an introduction to numerical computational software packages (e.g., MATLAB, SPSS), the use of computer programs in calculus and differential equations, and the application of numerical computation software to solve problems in numerical analysis.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to: • Recognize symbolic computational software packages, such as Mathematica, and numerical computational software packages. • Understand how to use a computer program for calculus and differential equations
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Explain various symbolic and numerical computational software packages, such as Mathematica, MATLAB, and SPSS. • Determine how to use computer programs to solve problems related to calculus and differential equations. Intellectual Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Analyze mathematical problems to identify the appropriate computational approach (symbolic or numerical) for solving them using software. • Interpret the results generated by computational software within the context of mathematical and scientific problems. Professional and Practical Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Apply computational software in calculus and solving differential equations. • Use numerical computation programs to solve practical problems in numerical analysis. Transferable Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Communicate effectively about statistical results. • Communicate effectively about the use of computational software and its results with colleagues and specialists. • Work efficiently as part of a team to solve complex problems that require the use of software tools

courses.courseDescription: The course content includes: the concept of a ring and subring (their properties and examples), ring homomorphism and isomorphism, integral domains and fields, the field of quotients of an integral domain (the rational field of an integral domain), prime fields and the characteristic of a ring, polynomial rings (division and greatest common divisor), roots of polynomials over a field, ideals and quotient rings, direct sums of rings and their properties, ring spaces and Euclidean rings, field extensions (simple and finite extensions of fields), algebraic closure of a field, splitting fields, and finite fields.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, the student will be able to: • Identify algebraic concepts and generalizations related to rings. • Deduce types of rings and operations on them.
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to: • Identify the concept of a ring, subring, and their properties. • Explain the relationships between homomorphism, ring isomorphism, and ideals. Cognitive Skills After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to: • Analyze the structure of integral domains, fields, and fields of quotients. • Distinguish between various types of field extensions, including simple and finite extensions. Professional and Practical Skills After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to: • Apply polynomial theories to calculate roots and the greatest common divisor. • Utilize concepts of prime fields and characteristics in constructing finite fields. General Transferable Skills After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to: • Manage time efficiently to complete tasks. • Work effectively in groups to solve complex problems

courses.courseDescription: The course's scientific content includes: Systems of Linear Equations and Matrices - Vectors in Two and Three Dimensions - General Vector Space - Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors - Matrix Diagonalization - Quadratic Form of Equations and Their Transformation to Canonical Form - Vector Spaces - Linear Independence - Dimensions and Basis Vectors of Spaces - Basis Transformation - Dot Product - Orthogonal Vectors - Linear Transformations, and their Applications
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, the student will be able to: • Understand systems of linear equations, matrices, and vectors in two and three dimensions. • Grasp the quadratic form of equations and orthogonal vectors. • Explain the quadratic form of equations and how to convert them into canonical form, in addition to concepts of vector spaces, linear independence, dimensions, and basis vectors for spaces
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding • Defines the fundamental concepts of linear equation systems, matrices, vectors in two and three dimensions, and general vector spaces. • Explains the meaning of eigenvalues and eigenvectors and how to transform a matrix into its diagonal form. • Describes the quadratic form of an equation and its transformation into canonical form, in addition to concepts of vector spaces, linear independence, dimensions, and basis vectors of spaces. Intellectual Skills • Analyzes complex linear equation systems and identifies the best methods for solving them using matrices. • Infers the relationships between vectors in different spaces and applies concepts of linear independence and dimensions. • Applies linear transformations in various contexts and interprets their applications in different fields. Professional and Practical Skills • Uses specialized mathematical software to calculate eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and transform matrices. • Performs dot products and orthogonal vector operations accurately and uses them to solve geometric problems. • Develops strategies for solving complex problems related to vector spaces and their transformations. General and Transferable Skills • Collaborates effectively with colleagues in solving group problems and exchanging ideas about linear algebra concepts. • Communicates clearly and effectively about complex mathematical concepts, both in writing and orally. Thinks critically and systematically when facing mathematical challenges in linear algebra and its applications

courses.courseDescription: The scientific content of this course includes: metric spaces and fundamental inequalities. It covers open and closed sets, convergence, spherical neighborhoods, closure of a set and its properties, and complete metric spaces. The course then moves to normed spaces, subspaces of a normed space, and equivalent norms. Regarding linear operators on a normed space, it defines the linear, continuous, and bounded operator, linear operators on finite-dimensional spaces, and the inverse of a linear operator. Finally, it covers inner product spaces and Hilbert spaces, orthogonal sets, the Riesz Representation Theorem, properties of linear and bounded operators between Hilbert spaces, and adjoint, self-adjoint, normal, and unitary operators
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to: • Identify metric spaces and normed spaces. • Determine the properties of linear operators in a normed space. • Explain Hilbert spaces and bounded operators in a Hilbert space
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Identify the fundamental concepts of metric spaces, normed spaces, complete spaces, and inner product spaces. • Explain the properties of linear operators (continuous, bounded, invertible) in normed spaces and Hilbert spaces. • Determine orthogonal sets in Hilbert spaces and adjoint, self-adjoint, normal, and unitary operators. Intellectual Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Analyze the relationships between open and closed sets and convergence in metric spaces. • Interpret Riesz Representation Theorem and the properties of bounded linear operators between two Hilbert spaces. • Distinguish between equivalent norms and their effect on the properties of normed spaces. Professional and Practical Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Apply fundamental inequalities in functional analysis to solve problems. • Use concepts of linear operators in finite-dimensional spaces to calculate the inverse of an operator. • Calculate the inner product of vectors to determine orthogonality in Hilbert spaces. Transferable Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Work efficiently as part of a team to discuss and clarify abstract concepts. • Communicate effectively with colleagues and specialists in discussions.

courses.courseDescription: The course content includes: wave-particle duality, wave packets, solving the Schrödinger equation for a free particle, solving the Schrödinger equation for a bound particle, quantum postulates, matrix mechanics, angular momentum, and spin.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, the student will be able to: • Identify the fundamental principles and postulates of quantum mechanics. • Deduce the definition of the wave function and its statistical interpretation. • Understand the concept of operators and the uncertainty principle, and how to solve the Schrödinger equation and special functions for a physical system.
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to: • Identify wave-particle duality and the concept of wave packets. • Explain quantum postulates and matrix mechanics. Cognitive Skills After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to: • Analyze solutions to the Schrödinger equation for both free and bound particles. • Differentiate between the concepts of angular momentum and spin in quantum systems. Professional and Practical Skills After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to: • Apply quantum principles to understand particle behavior at atomic and subatomic levels. • Utilize mathematical models to calculate the quantum properties of physical systems. General Transferable Skills After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to: • Discuss clearly with peers the challenges and paradoxes encountered. • Work efficiently within a team to explore solutions for complex problems.

courses.courseDescription: This course covers fundamental concepts in statistics and probability, beginning with data organization, summarization, and presentation through tables, including relative and percentage frequency tables for both qualitative and quantitative data. It then delves into graphical representation for both types of data, followed by an exploration of measures of central tendency, percentiles, and dispersion. The course also introduces the principles of probability, covering concepts such as sets, statistical experiments, sample space, events, operations on events, mutually exclusive events, exhaustive events, and equally likely outcomes. Further topics include conditional probability, independent events, the definition of a random variable, selected discrete probability distributions, and the normal distribution, concluding with an introduction to correlation and regression
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to: Understand, analyze, and apply statistical measures. Acquire knowledge and skills related to probability measures in quantitative and qualitative data across various fields
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Identify basic concepts in statistics and probability. • Explain the principles of probability. Intellectual Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Analyze statistical data presented in tables and graphs, and derive meaningful information from them. • Interpret appropriate statistical methods and probability principles for processing and solving data-related problems. Professional and Practical Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Apply statistical techniques to collect, organize, and present actual data using appropriate tools. • Calculate various statistical measures such as measures of central tendency, dispersion, and basic probabilities. • Organize data for presentation in tables. Transferable Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Communicate effectively about statistical results. • Present interpretations and conclusions clearly and systematically. • Work efficiently as part of a team to solve problems. • Participate actively in discussions

courses.courseDescription: The course content includes: electrostatic fields, their equations, and Gauss's Law in vacuum and dielectric materials; an introduction to conservative force fields, potential energy, and a study of electrostatic potential, Laplace's and Poisson's equations and their solutions; magnetic fields and their calculation, and Ampere's Law for magnetostatics; time-varying fields, Maxwell's equations, and the Law of Conservation of Charge; solving Maxwell's equations in vacuum, the propagation of electromagnetic waves in various media, magnetic power, the Poynting vector, and the electromagnetic wave spectrum
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, the student will be able to: • Grasp the principle of field theory and its unification, starting with the simplest fields: electric and magnetic fields, and understand Maxwell's equations
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding Level • Identifies the concepts of electrostatic fields and Gauss's Law. • Explains Maxwell's equations and the law of charge conservation. Cognitive Skills Level • Analyzes conservative force fields, potential energy, and electrostatic field potential. • Distinguishes between the propagation of electromagnetic waves in vacuum and various media. Professional and Practical Skills Level • Applies Laplace's and Poisson's equations to solve potential electrical problems. • Utilizes the Poynting vector to calculate magnetic power and electromagnetic wave energy. General Transferable Skills Level • Discusses complex scientific ideas clearly and effectively. • Collaborates effectively within a team to complete shared tasks

courses.courseDescription: The course's scientific content includes: Group Theory - Subgroups - Group Homomorphisms - Permutation Groups - Cyclic Groups - Group Isomorphism, and Quotient Groups - Geometric Transformation Groups - Rings, Ideals, and Quotient Rings - Subfields and Field Factorization - Algebraically Closed Fields - Integral Domains - Polynomials over a Field
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, you'll be able to: • Acquire fundamental concepts in modern algebra, including groups, rings, and fields. • Differentiate between rings, ideals, and quotient rings, and grasp the concept of fields. • Deduce the properties of permutation groups, cyclic groups, and the isomorphism between groups and quotient groups.
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding • Defines the fundamental concepts of Group Theory, Subgroups, and Homomorphisms between groups. • Explains the properties of Permutation Groups, Cyclic Groups, and the Isomorphism between groups and Quotient Groups. • Distinguishes between Rings, Ideals, and Quotient Rings, and understands the concept of Fields. Intellectual Skills • Analyzes problems related to groups and rings using appropriate mathematical theories and concepts. • Deduces new properties of algebraic structures based on given data and known theorems. • Applies abstract algebraic principles to solve complex mathematical problems concerning fields and integral domains. Professional and Practical Skills • Uses mathematical symbols and terminology accurately and effectively in scientific communication regarding abstract algebra. • Executes complex algebraic operations on groups, rings, and fields efficiently. • Identifies logical errors in proofs or mathematical solutions presented within an algebraic context. General and Transferable Skills • Collaborates effectively in solving group problems and exchanging mathematical ideas. • Communicates clearly and effectively about complex mathematical concepts, both in writing and orally. • Thinks critically and systematically when facing new mathematical challenges.

courses.courseDescription: This course's content includes: the concept of a function, its properties, operations on functions, types of functions, function composition, and inverse functions. It covers the concept of limits, properties of limits, the concept of a function's limit at infinity, and the concept of right-hand and left-hand limits, along with methods for calculating limits. The course also delves into the concept of continuity, its properties, and theorems on continuity. Furthermore, it examines the concept of differentiation, the relationship between differentiation and continuity, differentiation rules, trigonometric functions, derivatives of inverse trigonometric functions, hyperbolic functions, derivatives of inverse hyperbolic functions, derivatives of exponential and logarithmic functions, higher-order derivatives and Leibniz's Theorem, the chain rule, implicit differentiation, and parametric forms of functions, along with a study of some applications of differentiation. Finally, the course covers integration: integration of algebraic functions, integration of exponential and logarithmic functions, integration of trigonometric and inverse trigonometric functions, and integration of hyperbolic and inverse hyperbolic functions
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to: • Identify the concepts of functions and limits. • Grasp the concepts of continuity and differentiation, and determine their properties and relationships.
courses.courseOutcomes: knowledge and Understanding After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Define the concept of a function, its properties, types, and operations, including function composition and inverse functions. • Explain the concept of limits, their properties, methods of calculation, limits at infinity, and right-hand and left-hand limits. • Identify the concept of continuity, its properties, and related theorems. • Describe the concept of differentiation, its relationship with continuity, and the rules of differentiation for various functions. • Summarize the types of integrals for algebraic, trigonometric, hyperbolic, exponential, and logarithmic functions. Intellectual Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Analyze the behavior of functions as they approach specific points or infinity to determine their limits. • Interpret the relationship between higher-order derivatives and Leibniz's Theorem. • Distinguish between methods for differentiating implicit functions and parametric forms of functions. • Infer applications of differentiation in solving various mathematical problems. Professional and Practical Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Apply differentiation rules to trigonometric, hyperbolic, exponential, logarithmic, and inverse functions. • Use the chain rule and differentiation of implicit and parametric functions to calculate derivatives. • Calculate definite and indefinite integrals for algebraic, trigonometric, hyperbolic, exponential, and logarithmic functions. Transferable Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Formulate clear and organized solutions for mathematical problems in calculus. • Work efficiently as part of a team to discuss and clarify complex mathematical concepts. • Communicate effectively about mathematical methods and results with colleagues and supervisors

courses.courseDescription: The course's scientific content includes: Review of Simple Harmonic Motion - Damped Harmonic Motion - Examples and Applications of Damped Harmonic Motion - Central Orbits - Applications of Central Orbits - Kepler's Laws - Introduction to Space Dynamics - Circular Coordinate Systems - Motion Near the Earth's Surface and Foucault's Pendulum - Velocity and Acceleration in Circular Systems in Cylindrical Coordinates - Velocity and Acceleration in Circular Systems in Polar and Spherical Coordinates.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, you'll be able to: • Apply scientific facts and theories of particle dynamics. • Identify different patterns in particle dynamics
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding • Defines advanced concepts of simple and damped harmonic motion and their applications. • Explains the principles of central orbits and Kepler's Laws in dynamics. • Describes the fundamentals of space dynamics and how to calculate velocity and acceleration in cylindrical, polar, and spherical coordinates. Intellectual Skills • Analyzes complex problems related to damped harmonic motion and its applications in physical systems. • Infers kinematic relationships for objects in central orbits based on Kepler's Laws. • Applies laws of motion in space to calculate velocity and acceleration in various coordinate systems. Professional and Practical Skills • Uses appropriate mathematical equations to describe motion near the Earth's surface and determine the behavior of Foucault's pendulum. • Executes precise calculations for velocity and acceleration in cylindrical, polar, and spherical coordinates. • Develops problem-solving skills related to advanced dynamics and complex physical systems. General and Transferable Skills After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to: • Communicate effectively about statistical results. • Present interpretations and conclusions clearly and organized. • Work efficiently within a team to solve problems. • Participate effectively in discussions.

courses.courseDescription: The scientific content of this course includes: spatial statics, friction force and normal reaction, slipping and overturning, center of gravity, virtual work, stability of equilibrium, and reduction of force systems.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to: • Recognize the fundamental principles in statics. • Grasp information related to vector algebra, the weight of bodies and surfaces, and types of equilibrium.
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding After completing this course, students are expected to be able to: • Define fundamental concepts of spatial statics, friction force, and center of gravity. • Explain the principles of slipping, overturning, and equilibrium stability in statistical systems. Intellectual Skills After completing this course, students are expected to be able to: • Analyze the effect of friction force and normal reaction on the movement and equilibrium of bodies. • Interpret the principles of virtual work and the reduction of force systems within the context of statics. Professional and Practical Skills After completing this course, students are expected to be able to: • Apply the laws of spatial statics to calculate forces and torques in three dimensions. • Calculate friction coefficients and use them in analyzing the equilibrium of bodies prone to slipping or overturning. Transferable Skills After completing this course, students are expected to be able to: • Communicate effectively about statistical results. • Present interpretations and conclusions clearly and systematically. • Work efficiently as part of a team to solve problems. • Participate actively in discussions.

courses.courseTitle: Introduction to Number Theory and logic
courses.courseDescription: This course covers: numerical identities – linear congruence and the theory of residues – primitive roots and indices – quadratic residues, Legendre symbol, and the law of quadratic reciprocity – arithmetic functions – basic Diophantine equations – infinite continued fractions and rational approximations of real numbers – Pell’s equation – distribution of prime numbers
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be aware of the fundamental concepts of number theory, recognize key ideas in prime number theory and their relationship to algebraic number theory, appreciate the importance of number theory, and develop mathematical proof skills
courses.courseOutcomes: A) Knowledge and Understanding: After completing this course, students are expected to be able to:Identify the fundamental concepts of number theory, Understand arithmetic functions. B) Intellectual Skills: Students are expected to be able to: Analyze the distribution of prime numbers. , Apply the law of quadratic reciprocity. C) Professional and Practical Skills: Students are expected to be able to: Apply prime number theory. , Solve basic Diophantine equations. D) Transferable and Generic Skills: Students are expected to be able to: Organize and complete required tasks , Use arithmetic skills in everyday life.

courses.courseDescription: The course content includes: Coulomb’s law, Gauss’s theorem, electric field and lines of force, equipotential surface, electric dipole, Poisson’s and Laplace’s equations, Poisson transformations, solving Laplace equations, and the continuity equation.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to understand the fundamental concepts and theories in the fields of electricity, magnetism, and alternating current.
courses.courseOutcomes: A) Knowledge and Understanding: After completing this course, students are expected to be able to:State the fundamental theories in the field of electricity, Identify the basic concepts of magnetism. B) Cognitive Skills: After completing this course, students are expected to be able to: Differentiate between electric field intensity and lines of force. C) Practical and Professional Skills: After completing this course, students are expected to be able to: Apply Gauss’s theorem in relevant situations. D) Key Transferable Skills: After completing this course, students are expected to be able to: Use analytical skills, Solve related problems

courses.courseDescription: The course content includes: an introduction to Graph Theory, applications of the theory, vector forms/shapes, basic concepts and theories about forms/shapes, algorithms, shape theory, and computer programs.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, the student will be able to: • Identify the concepts of Graph Theory. • Deduce the concepts associated with Graph Theory. • Determine the uses of Graph Theory in studying mathematical graphs.
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to: • Identify the definition of basic concepts in Graph Theory. • Explain the applications of Graph Theory in various fields. Cognitive Skills After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to: • Analyze vector forms/shapes and their related theories. • Distinguish between different types of algorithms used in shape theory. ________________________________________ Professional and Practical Skills After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to: • Apply Graph Theory concepts to solve practical problems. • Utilize computer programs to study and analyze graphical forms/shapes. General Transferable Skills After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to: • Communicate effectively about complex ideas in mathematical theories. • Collaborate with colleagues in exploring challenges related to graph design and analysis

courses.courseDescription: The course content includes: an introduction to planetary mechanics and its applications, the motion of artificial satellites and spacecraft in space, orbital elements, converting orbital elements into position and velocity vectors, types of space orbits, and space orbit design.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, the student will be able to: • Understand planetary mechanics. • Grasp the applications of planetary mechanics, the motion of artificial satellites, and spacecraft in space.
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding Level • Identifies fundamental concepts of planetary mechanics and their applications. • Explains the motion of artificial satellites and spacecraft in space. Cognitive Skills Level • Analyzes orbital elements and their conversion into position and velocity vectors. • Distinguishes between different types of space orbits. Professional and Practical Skills Level • Applies engineering principles in the design of space orbits. • Utilizes acquired knowledge to simulate the motion of celestial bodies. General and Transferable Skills Level • Communicates clearly about complex aspects of planetary mechanics. • Collaborates within a team to explore space navigation challenges.

courses.courseDescription: The scientific content of this course includes: the concept of topology, definitions of topological spaces, closed and open sets, interior and boundary regions, first and second countability axioms, separable spaces, methods of generating topology on sets, interior and closure operators, bases and sub-bases, subspaces, Cartesian products, sums, embedding, local embedding, and metrizable topological spaces.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to: • Identify the concept of topology, topological spaces, Cartesian products, and metrizable topological spaces. • Grasp interpretations of topology and various topological spaces, as well as open and closed sets. • Infer interior and closure operators, bases and sub-bases, and the concepts of local embedding and metrizable spaces.
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Identify the concept of topology and various topological spaces, as well as open and closed sets. • Explain the first and second countability axioms, separable spaces, and methods for generating topology on sets. • Determine interior and closure operators, bases and sub-bases, and the concepts of local embedding and metrizable spaces. Intellectual Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Analyze the properties of spherical neighborhoods and the closure of sets in topological spaces. • Interpret the relationship between Cartesian products, sums, and embedding within the context of topological spaces. • Distinguish between different types of topological spaces based on their properties (e.g., complete and metrizable spaces). Professional and Practical Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Apply topological concepts to determine the interior and boundary regions of a given set. • Use rules for generating topology to construct new topologies on given sets. • Calculate convergence properties in various topological spaces.

courses.courseDescription: The course content includes: vectors in space, various forms of the equation of a straight line in space, the vector and parametric equations of a space curve, the relationship between two straight lines in space (parallelism, intersection, skew lines), the equation of a plane in space, the equation of a family of planes, the relationship between a straight line and a plane, the intersection of two planes in space, equations of surfaces of revolution in space (solids of conic surfaces, the sphere, the cone), and the intersection of planes with space surfaces
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, the student will be able to: • Identify vectors in space and the different forms of the equation of a straight line in space. • Understand the vector and parametric equations of a space curve. • Deduce the relationship between two straight lines in space
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to: • Identify the concept of vectors in space and the different forms of equations for straight lines and planes. • Explain the relationship between straight lines and planes in space. Cognitive Skills After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to: • Analyze the geometric relationships between lines, planes, and surfaces of revolution in space. • Differentiate between the various types of intersections of planes with space surfaces. Professional and Practical Skills After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to: • Apply vector and parametric equations to describe curves and space surfaces. • Utilize concepts of spatial geometry to solve engineering and scientific problems. General Transferable Skills After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to: • Discuss complex mathematical ideas and concepts clearly with colleagues. • Work effectively within a team to analyze and solve engineering problems.

courses.courseDescription: The course includes the following topics: solving second-order differential equations, Bessel and Legendre equations, Laplace transform method, systems of equations, existence and uniqueness theorems for first- and second-order differential equations, finite difference equations, and first-order partial differential equations.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, the student will be able to understand first-order and first-degree differential equations, various types of linear differential equations, and distinguish between the fundamental theories of ordinary differential equations.
courses.courseOutcomes: A) Knowledge and Understanding: After completing this course, students are expected to be able to:Identify the order of differential equations,Recognize the existence and uniqueness theorem. B) Intellectual Skills: Students are expected to be able to:Distinguish between linear differential equations,Compare the fundamental theories of ordinary differential equations. C) Professional and Practical Skills: Students are expected to be able to:Solve linear differential equations.,Solve first- and second-order differential equations. D) Transferable and Generic Skills: Students are expected to be able to:Manage time effectively,Apply scientific thinking.

courses.courseDescription: The course covers the following topics: the concept of system and surroundings, types of systems, types of processes in thermodynamics (isothermal and adiabatic processes), extensive and intensive properties, the concept of free energy, enthalpy, and entropy, the zeroth law of thermodynamics and the reason behind its name, the first law of thermodynamics, work, the relationship between CVC_VCV and CPC_PCP, Hess's law, entropy as a state function, laws of chemical kinetics, rate laws, calculation of reaction rates and rate constants, rate expressions, stoichiometric measurements, reaction order, concentration profiles for reactions, integrated rate equations for simple reactions, quantitative studies of half-life times for different reactions, pseudo-order reactions, zero-order reactions, and general order reactions
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to identify various thermodynamic laws that explain chemical kinetics using data analysis methods, equations, and theoretical frameworks.
courses.courseOutcomes: A) Knowledge and Understanding: After completing this course, students are expected to be able to:Define the concept of a system and its surroundings ,Identify extensive and intensive properties., Explain the concepts of free energy, enthalpy, and entropy. B) Intellectual Skills: Students are expected to be able to:Analyze the laws of chemical kinetics.,Use rate laws and calculate reaction rates and rate constants. C) Professional and Practical Skills: Students are expected to be able to:Analyze the concentration profile of reactions.,Apply integrated rate equations for simple reactions. D) Transferable and Generic Skills: Students are expected to be able to :Evaluate information .,Manage time and set priorities ,Meet deadlines

courses.courseDescription: The course's scientific content includes: Cartesian, Cylindrical, and Spherical Coordinates - Functions of Two Variables - Functions of Three Variables - Limits - Continuity - Partial Derivatives - Chain Rule - Extreme Values of Functions of Two Variables - Lagrange Multipliers - Double Integrals and their Applications - Double Integrals in Polar Coordinates - Triple Integrals and their Applications - Triple Integrals in Cylindrical and Spherical Coordinates - Sequences - Infinite Series - Convergence Tests - Representation of Functions by Power Series - Taylor and Maclaurin Series, and Binomial Series.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, you'll be able to: • Generalize single-variable function concepts to multivariable functions. • Identify various applications of functions. • Describe the concept of extreme values and functions of two variables using Lagrange multipliers, along with different types of multiple integrals (double and triple) in various coordinate systems
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding • Defines the fundamental concepts of Cartesian, cylindrical, and spherical coordinate systems, as well as functions of two and three variables. • Explains the concepts of limits, continuity, partial derivatives, and the chain rule in the context of multivariable functions. • Describes the concept of extreme values and functions of two variables using Lagrange multipliers, in addition to various types of multiple integrals (double and triple) in different coordinate systems. Intellectual Skills • Analyzes the behavior of multivariable functions at critical points and determines their extreme values. • Infers the convergence or divergence of sequences and infinite series using various convergence tests. • Applies double and triple integrals to solve geometric and physical problems, and utilizes them in polar, cylindrical, and spherical coordinates. Professional and Practical Skills • Uses series (such as power series, Taylor, and Maclaurin series) to represent and approximate functions. • Executes complex partial differentiation operations and multiple integrals with accuracy. • Develops strategies for solving problems involving coordinate transformations and the calculation of Lagrange multipliers. General and Transferable Skills • Collaborates effectively in solving complex problems related to multivariable calculus. • Communicates clearly and effectively about mathematical concepts and theories in calculus, both in writing and orally. • Thinks critically and systematically when dealing with new mathematical challenges in this field.

courses.courseDescription: The course's scientific content includes: Basic Concepts in Analytical Dynamics - Lagrange's Equations for Holonomic Dynamical Systems - Derivation of Lagrange's Equations and Definition of the Lagrangian Function - Atwood Machine and Real-Life Applications - Hamilton's Function and Derivation of Hamilton's Equations - Jacobi Integrals and Hamilton's Principle - Derivation of Hamilton's Equations using Hamilton's Principle - Poisson Brackets - Proof of Jacobi-Poisson Theorem - Equilibrium Position
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, you'll be able to: • Identify theories and laws in analytical dynamics. • Derive methods for data analysis, equations, and theories. • Recognize real-life applications of analytical dynamics.
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding • Defines the fundamental concepts in analytical dynamics and the theory of Lagrange's equations. • Explains the Lagrangian and Hamiltonian functions and how to derive Hamilton's equations. • Describes Jacobi integrals and Hamilton's principle, as well as Poisson brackets and the Jacobi-Poisson theorem. Intellectual Skills • Analyzes holonomic dynamical systems and applies Lagrange's and Hamilton's equations to them. • Infers the equilibrium position of complex dynamical systems using analytical principles. • Applies theoretical concepts in analytical dynamics to solve real-life application examples. Professional and Practical Skills • Uses mathematical principles to derive equations of motion for physical systems. • Executes equation derivations and calculates Poisson brackets with accuracy. • Develops mathematical proof skills to demonstrate theorems such as the Jacobi-Poisson theorem. General and Transferable Skills • Communicates effectively about statistical results. • Presents interpretations and conclusions clearly and in an organized manner. • Works efficiently within a team to solve problems. • Participates effectively in discussions.

courses.courseDescription: The scientific content of this course includes: sampling distributions and the Central Limit Theorem. It covers point estimation and the properties of estimators (unbiasedness, mean squared error, consistency, sufficiency, minimal sufficiency). The course also delves into the exponential family, the Cramér-Rao inequality, Fisher information, the Rao-Blackwell Theorem (sufficiency and completeness), and the Lehmann-Scheffé Theorem. Estimation methods covered include the method of moments and maximum likelihood estimators with their asymptotic properties. It also explores the use of prior density functions, invariance methods, interval estimation, confidence interval estimators, pivotal methods, and Bayesian credible intervals.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to: • Identify important statistical methods and concepts related to hypothesis testing, parameter estimation, and confidence intervals for these parameters. • Recognize theories and properties associated with probability theory
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Identify fundamental concepts in mathematical statistics, such as sampling distributions, properties of estimators, and the Central Limit Theorem. • Explain the relationship between the Cramér-Rao inequality and Fisher information, as well as the Rao-Blackwell and Lehmann-Scheffé theorems. Intellectual Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Analyze the properties of different estimators (unbiasedness, consistency, sufficiency) to assess their efficiency. • Interpret results derived from point and interval estimation methods, and confidence intervals for population parameters. Professional and Practical Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Apply various estimation methods, such as the method of moments and maximum likelihood estimators, to calculate parameter estimates. • Calculate confidence intervals for population parameters using pivotal methods and Bayesian credible intervals. Transferable Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Communicate effectively about statistical results. • Formulate logical arguments regarding the selection of the most appropriate statistical estimators for a given situation. • Work within a team to discuss challenges in statistical estimation and develop solutions for them

courses.courseDescription: This course's scientific content includes: the concept of inferential statistics; sampling theory, its importance and applications in society; the normal distribution and standard normal distribution, along with the table of critical values for the standard normal distribution. It also covers the chi-square distribution, theories explaining its relationship to the normal distribution, applied examples, and its critical values table. The course introduces the t-distribution, theories explaining its relationship to the normal distribution, applied examples, and its values table. Additionally, it examines the F-distribution, theories explaining its relationship to the normal distribution, applied examples, and its values table. Key topics also include the definition, importance, and practical applications of hypothesis testing, specifically chi-square, t-tests, and F-tests. Finally, the course defines simple and complex analysis of variance and simple linear regression.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to: • Identify concepts and principles related to inferential statistics. • Grasp the principles of inferential statistics and their real-life applications
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Define the concept of inferential statistics and the importance of sampling theory and its applications. • Explain the differences between the normal distribution, standard normal distribution, and the chi-square, t, and F distributions. Intellectual Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Analyze the relationship between different statistical distributions (such as the normal distribution and chi-square, t, F). • Interpret the results of statistical hypothesis tests and simple and complex analysis of variance. Professional and Practical Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Apply statistical hypothesis tests (such as chi-square, t, F tests) to various data sets. • Calculate simple linear regression coefficients and use them for prediction. Transferable Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Present interpretations and conclusions systematically. • Work efficiently as part of a team to solve problems

courses.courseDescription: The scientific content of this course includes: complex numbers, polar representation, complex functions, limits, continuity, analytic functions, elementary complex functions (trigonometric, hyperbolic, exponential, logarithmic, and complex power functions), differentiation, definite integrals, complex line integrals, infinite series, Taylor series, Laurent series, Residue Theorem, applications in real and improper integrals, and physical and engineering applications, as well as Cauchy's Integral Theorem.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to: • Recognize the importance of using numerical methods to solve a variety of scientific problems. • Explain interpolation methods, numerical integration and differentiation, and matrix analysis methods. • Identify the fundamental principles for solving systems of linear equations and ordinary differential equations. • Apply numerical methods to solve various scientific problems, finding approximate solutions to the problems presented in different fields
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Define complex numbers and their various representations, including polar representation. • Explain the concepts of limits, continuity, and analytic functions in complex analysis. • Identify elementary complex functions such as trigonometric, hyperbolic, exponential, logarithmic, and complex power functions. • Describe Cauchy's Residue and Integral Theorems, and the concepts of infinite series, Taylor series, and Laurent series. Intellectual Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Analyze the properties of complex functions to determine their differentiability and analyticity. • Interpret the relationship between complex analysis and its applications in real and improper integrals. • Distinguish between different types of infinite series in the complex plane and their convergence properties. Professional and Practical Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Apply differentiation and integration rules to complex functions. • Use the Residue Theorem to calculate complex line integrals and complex real integrals. • Compute Taylor and Laurent series expansions for complex functions around specific points. Transferable Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Formulate mathematical and engineering problems that require the use of complex analysis. • Work efficiently within a team to discuss and clarify complex concepts in complex analysis. Communicate effectively about mathematical methods and results with colleagues and specialists

courses.courseDescription: The scientific content of this course includes: linear programming (graphical and algebraic methods, the simplex method, dual simplex method, and parametric analysis), error analysis, transportation problems and the transportation model, and integer programming (cutting plane method, linear analysis, branch and bound method). It also covers dynamic programming and various solution methods using dynamic programming.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to: • Identify concepts related to the science of operations research, such as linear programming. • Grasp linear analysis, dynamic programming, and solution methods using dynamic programming.
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding After completing this course, students are expected to be able to: • Identify fundamental concepts in operations research, such as linear programming, parametric analysis, and integer programming. • Explain various solution methods in linear programming (graphical, algebraic, and simplex methods) and dynamic programming. Intellectual Skills After completing this course, students are expected to be able to: • Analyze linear programming problems using the simplex method, dual simplex method, and parametric analysis. • Interpret the results of linear and dynamic analysis to derive optimal decisions. Professional and Practical Skills After completing this course, students are expected to be able to: • Apply graphical, algebraic, and simplex methods to solve linear programming and transportation problems. • Calculate solutions for dynamic programming and integer programming problems using appropriate methods. Transferable Skills After completing this course, students are expected to be able to: • Formulate real-world problems into mathematical models solvable using operations research. • Work efficiently as part of a team to solve complex problems requiring mathematical models and quantitative analysis.

courses.courseDescription: The course's scientific content includes: Biomathematics: Concept and Importance - Mathematical Modeling - Dynamical Systems as Differential Equations - Optimal Formulas for Solutions of Dynamical Differential Equations - Growth Equations - Competition for Fixed Resources - Applications of Exponential Functions in Biology - Time-Concentration Curves in Blood Injected with Drugs via Separation - Common Growth Functions - Exponential Curves - Time Period for Retaining Carbon Dioxide in the Lungs During Respiration - Measurement of Cardiac Output - Communication Science and Insufficiency - Differential Equations for Epidemics - Bacteriology - Mechanism of Reproduction and Extinction - Membrane Diffusion
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, you'll be able to: • Understand differential equations and mathematical modeling for comprehending biological systems. • Describe how to measure cardiac output, the mechanisms of bacterial reproduction and extinction, and the concept of membrane diffusion. • Explain the growth function and the applications of exponential functions in biology.
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding • Defines the concept and importance of biomathematics, along with the principles of mathematical modeling for dynamical systems as differential equations. • Explains the growth function, the concept of competition for fixed resources, and the applications of exponential functions in biology. • Describes how to measure cardiac output, the mechanisms of bacterial reproduction and extinction, and the concept of membrane diffusion. Intellectual Skills • Analyzes time-concentration curves in drug-injected blood to extract biological information. • Infers optimal formulas for solutions of dynamical differential equations applied in biological systems. • Applies differential equations to model epidemics and understand their dynamics. Professional and Practical Skills • Uses common functions (like exponential functions) to represent growth and decay phenomena in biology. • Executes calculations related to the time period for retaining carbon dioxide in the lungs during respiration. • Develops simple mathematical models to describe bacterial reproduction and extinction mechanisms, and membrane diffusion. General and Transferable Skills • Communicates effectively about statistical results. • Presents interpretations and conclusions clearly and in an organized manner. • Works efficiently within a team to solve problems. • Participates effectively in discussions

courses.courseDescription: The scientific content of this course includes: periodic functions – binary functions – monotonic functions – limits – chain rule – mean value theorem – Leibniz’s theorem – Taylor series – Maclaurin series – homogeneous functions – Euler’s theorem for homogeneous functions – improper integrals – sets – subsets – cyclic groups – groups – Lagrange’s theorem – group symmetries – vectors – scalar product – rigid body – moments – couples – equilibrium – center of gravity – vector operators (gradient of a scalar function, divergence of a vector field, curl of a vector) – Stokes' theorem – velocity – acceleration – relative velocity – impulse – driving force – polar coordinates – simple harmonic motion – sample space – events – probability – permutations – combinations – conditional probability
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to explain concepts, facts, and principles in pure and applied mathematics, and statistics, and identify related theories and laws in English.
courses.courseOutcomes: A) Knowledge and Understanding: After studying this course, each student is expected to be able to:Name the different types of functions in English,State the various function-related theorems in English. B) Cognitive Skills: After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to:Differentiate between the principles of pure and applied mathematics in English.,Interpret the various functions in English. C) Practical and Professional Skills: After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to:Apply the principles of pure and applied mathematics ,Utilize various theorems in teaching mathematics in English. D) Key Transferable Skills: After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to:Motivate themselves to seek out information and expand their mathematical knowledge in English beyond the course content.

courses.courseDescription: The course covers physical and mechanical problems and integral equations, linear integral equations, classification and solutions of differential and integral equations, Fredholm integral equations of the first and second kind, Volterra integral equations of the first and second kind, characteristic behavior of integral equations, and applications to ordinary differential equations.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to understand various methods for solving Fredholm and Volterra integral equations.
courses.courseOutcomes: A) Knowledge and Understanding: After completing this course, students are expected to be able to:Classify differential and integral equations,Identify the characteristic behavior of integral equations. B) Intellectual Skills: Students are expected to be able to:Distinguish between first- and second-kind Volterra integral equations. C) Professional and Practical Skills: Students are expected to be able to:Apply integral equations to ordinary differential equations,Solve integral equations. D) Transferable and Generic Skills: Students are expected to be able to:Analyze data, Demonstrate new skills.

courses.courseDescription: The course content includes: Local Curve Theory: curvature, torsion, Serret-Frenet formulas (or Frenet-Serret theory), existence and uniqueness theorem for curves. Plane Curves: non-isometric, four-vertex theorem, rotation. Local Surface Theory: first fundamental form, normal and geodesic curvature, parallelism, second fundamental form, Weingarten maps, types of curvature, and constant curvature surfaces.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, the student will be able to: • Understand the local theory of curves • Analyze planar curves and identify the four-vertex theorem • Describe surface theory and fundamental forms
courses.courseOutcomes: A) Knowledge and Understanding: Upon successful completion of the course, students will be able to: • Explain the local theory of surfaces • Summarize the existence and uniqueness theorem of curves B) Intellectual Skills: Students will be able to: • Classify Weingarten maps • Distinguish between normal and geodesic curvature C) Professional and Practical Skills: Students will be able to: • Apply the local theory of curves • Analyze different types of curvature D) Transferable Skills: Students will be able to: • Analyze data • Collaborate effectively with peers • Use scientific research skills

courses.courseDescription: The course content includes: Introduction to Special Relativity, postulates of Special Relativity and Lorentz transformations, relativistic kinematics, geometrical representation of Special Relativity and Minkowski space, relativistic mechanics, Einstein's energy equation and various results, applications of Special Relativity (mechanical applications, applications in modern physics, and applications in chemistry)
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, the student will be able to: • Identify the scientific facts and concepts of the Theory of Relativity. • Deduce examples of applications of the Theory of Relativity
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding Level • Identifies the postulates of Special Relativity and Lorentz transformations. • Explains the concept of Minkowski space and the geometrical representation of Special Relativity. Cognitive Skills Level • Analyzes relativistic kinematics and mechanics. • Distinguishes between the different applications of Special Relativity in physics and chemistry. Professional and Practical Skills Level • Applies Einstein's energy equation to solve physical problems. • Utilizes the principles of Relativity Theory in interpreting modern phenomena. General Transferable Skills Level • Communicates clearly and effectively with others. • Collaborates effectively within a team to accomplish shared tasks

courses.courseDescription: The course includes the following topics: fundamental concepts, stress theory, equilibrium equations, principal stress surfaces, stress theory, stress conditions, fundamental stress components, strain energy, the relationship between stress and strain components (Hooke’s Law), fundamental problems in elasticity, Lame’s equations, Beltrami’s equations, plane stress, and plane strain.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, the student will be able to identify the scientific facts and theories of elasticity, effectively apply information technology related to elasticity theory, and select appropriate solutions for basic and specific equations of elasticity theory
courses.courseOutcomes: A) Knowledge and Understanding: After completing this course, students are expected to be able to:Define stress and strain theory,State the conditions of stress. B) Intellectual Skills: Students are expected to be able to:Analyze stress conditions and fundamental stress components, Compare scientific theories of elasticity. C) Professional and Practical Skills: Students are expected to be able to:Apply elasticity theory, Solve fundamental problems in elasticity. D) Transferable and Generic Skills: Students are expected to be able to:Use information technology, Develop innovative solutions.

courses.courseTitle: Information and Communication Technologies in Education and Research
courses.courseDescription: The course covers the principles of computer science, concepts of e-learning, and interaction with the university's educational platforms such as Learning Management Systems (LMS) and Student Information Systems (SIS). It aims to enhance students' skills and abilities to communicate effectively online and complete academic assignments. The course also includes concepts of artificial intelligence, the Internet of Things, and cybersecurity, as well as the use of the internet in education and scientific research.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Acquire foundational knowledge in Information and Communication Technology (ICT) and its applications in the field of education. • Develop study skills and enhance knowledge of fundamental computer systems applications and big data.
courses.courseOutcomes: A. Knowledge & Understanding At the end of the module, each student will be expected to: - Explain the principles of computer science. - Clarify e-learning concepts. B. Cognitive Skills At the end of the module, each student will be expected to: - Engage with the university’s educational platforms. - Distinguish between the concepts of artificial intelligence, the Internet of Things, and cybersecurity. C. Practical and Professional Skills At the end of the module, each student will be expected to: - Utilize the internet in educational contexts. - Use information technology in scientific research. D. Key Transferable Skills At the end of the module, each student will be expected to: - Develop scientific research skills.

courses.courseTitle: Introduction to Art and Design in Context
courses.courseDescription: This module provides generic and subject specific contextualization for undergraduate study in Art and Design. This module enables you to develop appropriate key skills including research and academic writing. You will be introduced to subject relevant social, historical and cultural contexts. These contexts will be presented through a variety of ways such as visual presentations, film and gallery visits.
courses.courseObjectives: Aims of the module: The aims of the design basics component of the course are: • Acquire the theory necessary for the practice of design • Discern the elements and principles of design • Recognize and appreciate design in nature and all creation • Acquire the basic terminology of the design profession • Develop an understanding of "why to do it" as well as "how to do it" • Appreciate the styles and mannerisms, past and present, in design and to know what makes their uniqueness • Acquire technical proficiency in the use of the tools and materials of design • Apply the elements and principles of design to given problems and to exploit their use for one's own creative inspirations.
courses.courseOutcomes: A. Knowledge and understanding: A1. Get familiar with the design elements: color, shape, line, tone, texture, form, etc. A2. Define the visual rolls of design principles: balance, contrast, cropping, etc. in design. A3. Identify the design elements and principles that satisfy the stated purpose. A4. Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the role of illustration as a communication tool in graphic and multimedia design. A5. Research, analyze, identify, and apply key aspects of the subject matter, the artistic techniques and the principles of drawing. A6. Use appropriate terminology to describe illustration types, styles, mediums, techniques and processes. A7. Explain, discuss and critique illustration artwork, including some reference to the art historical, social, and cultural context B. Cognitive Skills: B1. Adopt a creative approach to problem solving and to become self-critical in the editing of the design work. B2. Read text materials and identify key points and concepts that should or could be communicated through an illustration. B3. Select data and information from various sources and analyze and present them on an appropriate manner to support a project and its solution. B4. Communicate effectively visual concepts showing recognition of the target audience and the purpose of the illustrations. B5. Identify key elements of the subject matter needed to be illustrated and its purpose and identify the appropriate artistic techniques and methods for producing illustration projects. B6. Enrich skills of combining manual methodologies and materials in order to fulfill certain functions. C. Practical and professional Skills: C1. Solve design problems by using new visual solutions – systematic approaches. C2. Develop the ability to synthesize into a coherent point of view and communicate it through 2D and 3D formats. C3. Employ technical and artistic skills needed to create highly crafted illustration projects that communicate ideas for specific target audience and for various design applications. C4. Use effectively and creatively elements and principles of design in the creation of illustration projects. C5. Identify and communicate visually alternative solutions. C6. Create effective art composition by applying design principles and appropriate rules of composition. D. Key/ transferable Skills: D1. Translate verbal meanings into design forms, by using different materials and methodologies. D2. Discuss your work and the work of others with confidence and to offer critical feedback to their classmates. D3. Design, illustrate, and complete individual projects for various purposes and audience in an effective and creative manner. D4. Create a portfolio of graphic design and multimedia projects and display finished works in a professional manner. D5. Classify illustrations according to types of design problems, subject matter and applications. D6. Demonstrate an understanding of the demands and expectations of the illustration profession.

courses.courseTitle: Studio Practice Ideas, concepts and communication methods
courses.courseDescription: This module is studied in conjunction with the two other Studio Practice modules in Level 4 and the combination of these modules is intended to introduce you to the fundamentals of Visual Communication practice. A series of exploratory projects, lectures, seminars and workshops will introduce you to a number of strategies that will help you to generate ideas, concepts and delivery methods. You will understand the necessary verbal and visual skills required to communicate these concepts. Through this module you will acquire understanding of creative thinking, problem solving, concept development and communication strategies, you will record and evaluate your progress through a journal and/or sketchbook. Continuous Feedback will be delivered in the form of group and individual tutorials, discussions and debate.
courses.courseObjectives: Aims of the module: This studio-based course aims to develop students understanding of the fundamentals of visual language and design principles. The course provides students with a core knowledge base from which students can build visual problem-solving skills and enhance the ability to plan, create and critically evaluate processes. Students are introduced to visual communication and through the use of basic design strategies and media students will develop an understanding of core principles which underpin effective visual communication and factors which contribute to the creation of meaningful graphics forms. - This course enables students to: 1. Use visual art perceptions as an instrument for graphic design 2. Establish a positive work ethic in Graphic Design theory and practice 3. Participate in critiques; to begin to understand the importance of dialogue in the creative process 4. Learn about the professional practices of being a creative person 5. Understand graphic design as a tool for communicating information, concepts and emotions 6. Apply the elements and principles of design in their own graphic design endeavours 7. Discuss the impact of commercial art in today's society 8. Realize the implication and application at various media and their functions in graphic design Critically evaluate, develop arguments and demonstrate effective communication skills in the presentation of ideas and visual solutions.
courses.courseOutcomes: A. Knowledge and understanding: A1. Understand contemporary visual communication concepts, media and images, and their role in contemporary society. A2. Understand the graphic design functions of relating ideas, objects, and materials. A3. Explore and gain understanding of visual logic A4. Hands-on experiences that provide students opportunities to think and create visual messages. B. Cognitive Skills: B1. Develop critical thinking skills regarding the ways contemporary visual media shapes societal attitudes and behaviors. B2. Skill development in producing efficient visual communication messages B3. Develop mature understanding of the relationship between visual form and meaning B4. Achieve different approaches in graphic design to solving problems and be able to communicate results accurately with structured and coherent arguments. C. Practical and professional Skills: C1. Employ self-selected creative thinking and problem-solving techniques in a wide range of practical settings and situations. C2. Collaborate effectively in creative thinking and design problem-solving. D. Key/ transferable Skills: D1. Deal with complex issues, generate concepts and successfully communicate ideas through visual, written and/or oral means. D2. Adapt the learned information that affected the historical evolution of graphic design to today’s changing technologies.

courses.courseDescription: This module is intended to introduce the student to the fundamentals of Visual Communication practice. It will enable students to refine their drawing skills with visual elements and compositions, through the use of specialized software tools. Additional challenges are added that partner original thought with learned practices. In addition, this module introduces students to fundamental principles and applications of design, emphasizing critical and cultural awareness of design issues and developing technical skills. The notion of creative problem solving is particularly emphasized. Students develop expertise in major industry standard software packages. This module lays the foundation for further study of design. A broad range of hands-on delivered projects with emphasis on process, both traditional and digital, will enhance the student understanding of the potential of delivery methods and systems and provide the student with a working knowledge of and opportunities to further explore the application of these systems within their practice. Formative feedback will be delivered throughout the module in the form of group and individual tutorials, discussions and debates
